title: UK's Iconic Jodrell Bank Observatory Faces Closure After Government Pulls Funding
excerpt: Scientists, artists and politicians rally to save the UNESCO World Heritage site as UKRI withdraws £2.8 million annual budget for e-MERLIN telescope network, threatening nearly 70 years of radio astronomy.
body:
• UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) has withdrawn funding for e-MERLIN, the radio telescope network headquartered at Jodrell Bank, with the £2.8 million annual budget ending in March 2028.
  • The 76-metre Lovell Telescope — a UNESCO World Heritage site that tracked Sputnik in 1957 — could cease all scientific observations, putting 28 jobs at risk and affecting nearly 3,000 researchers.
  • Scientists warn the closure would also compromise Britain's national security, as the telescope has demonstrated a unique ability to track hostile satellites in geostationary orbit.
  • The cuts are part of a broader 2.7% reduction in UK astronomy, nuclear and particle physics research, with nearly 80% of early-career physicists considering leaving the country.

Britain's Jodrell Bank Observatory, home to the country's largest telescope for nearly seven decades, faces closure after the government's research funding body announced it would withdraw support for the site's most significant scientific project.

UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) confirmed that funding for e-MERLIN — a network of seven radio telescopes across England headquartered at Jodrell Bank in Cheshire — would end in March 2028. The decision eliminates the observatory's £2.8 million annual budget and, unless alternative funding is found, could silence the iconic 76-metre Lovell Telescope permanently.

A Growing Campaign to Save the Observatory

The announcement has triggered a wave of opposition from scientists, artists, writers and politicians who argue the funding cut amounts to national self-harm. Professor Brian Cox, the University of Manchester physicist and broadcaster, called the decision "hasty, ill-considered and devastating."

"These devastating and irreversible cuts are a legacy from a series of hasty and ill-considered decisions taken by UKRI, overseen by a government department that no longer exists."

— Professor Brian Cox, University of Manchester

Cox argued the cuts were inherited from decisions made before Andy Burnham became prime minister and disbanded the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, which had overseen UKRI. George Dransfield, an astrophysicist and Sky at Night presenter, called the cuts "a gamble on the future of UK science."

Royal Astronomical Society President Professor Jim Wild described the news as "devastating for UK astronomy," writing that "discarding unique, globally significant observatories threatens both our scientific future and the inspiration of future generations of astronomers." Scotland's Astronomer Royal, Professor Catherine Heymans, called the UKRI decision "a real act of national self-harm," according to the BBC.

Defence and Security Implications

The campaign to save Jodrell Bank extends beyond scientific and cultural arguments. Senior international scientists have warned that Britain risks losing a cutting-edge ability to track hostile satellites if the Lovell Telescope ceases operating.

Professor Marco Martorella, a radar expert at the University of Birmingham, told The Times that by pairing American radar transmitters with Jodrell Bank's highly sensitive receivers, an international team tracked objects as small as a football in geostationary orbit — about 22,000 miles above the Earth.

"There is no single radar in the world that can do that. Not even the best equipment the US has can do that by itself."

— Professor Marco Martorella, University of Birmingham

Martorella and his colleagues are set to receive NATO's Science and Technology Excellence Award for this work. Tony Beasley, director of the US National Radio Astronomy Observatory, described the research as "at the bleeding edge" and urged Britain to recognise the telescope as sovereign infrastructure.

Part of a Broader Squeeze on UK Science

The Jodrell Bank decision is part of a 2.7% cut to the UK's Particle Physics, Astronomy and Nuclear Physics budget over four years. Other casualties include withdrawal of funding for the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope in Hawaii, cuts to British involvement in the Extremely Large Telescope in Chile, and a 20% reduction in support for the Vera Rubin Telescope.

Professor Simon Garrington, the observatory's associate director, said the loss of e-MERLIN funding would "pull the rug out" from under Jodrell Bank's scientific work. He told BBC News that everyone at the observatory was "devastated" and warned that ending support would disperse the engineers and researchers needed for defence applications.

The funding squeeze has broader consequences for the UK's scientific workforce. According to The Times, nearly 80% of early-career physicists are now considering leaving Britain to pursue research abroad — a brain drain that could undermine the country's long-term competitiveness in science and technology.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indian-origin researchers and students in the UK — a significant contingent in British academia and STEM fields — the cuts signal growing uncertainty about the country's commitment to fundamental research. India's own space and radio astronomy programmes, including the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune, have been expanding. The contrast between Britain's retreat from radio astronomy and India's investment in it may influence where the next generation of scientists from the diaspora choose to build their careers.

What Happens Next

UKRI said the present e-MERLIN agreement would continue until March 2028, giving the University of Manchester time to find alternative funding. The agency emphasised it would continue supporting Jodrell Bank's role as headquarters of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, an international project building next-generation radio telescopes in South Africa and Australia, to which Britain will contribute about £327 million over a decade.

Macclesfield MP Tim Roca has pledged to make the case "for protecting this world-leading scientific institution." Garrington said the leadership team would challenge the decision and, if that fails, seek alternative funding to keep the Lovell Telescope operational in some form.

Founded in 1945 by Sir Bernard Lovell, Jodrell Bank became famous when the Lovell Telescope tracked the rocket carrying Sputnik into orbit in 1957. It earned UNESCO World Heritage status in 2019. The saving from closing it — £2.8 million annually — amounts to roughly five minutes of Britain's £350 billion welfare spending, according to The Times.
